Most beginners start with **glass and faceted crystal-style beads**, because they look good, are easy to find and are not too expensive. Keep natural stone and coral for later, when you can tell real material from imitation and can afford mistakes.
How beads are measured

Most beads are measured in **millimetres (mm)** across the widest part. A 4 mm bead is about the size of a peppercorn, an 8 mm bead is about the size of a chickpea, and 12 mm and above are bold statement beads. Oval and tube beads are given two numbers, such as 6 x 9 mm (width x length).

**Seed beads** use a different system called the aught size, written like 11/0 (say "eleven aught"). The bigger the number, the smaller the bead. As a rough guide, 15/0 is about 1.5 mm, 11/0 about 2 mm, 8/0 about 3 mm and 6/0 about 4 mm. Sizes vary a little between makers, so buy the same brand when you need beads to match exactly.
Check the hole, not only the bead

Two beads of the same size can have very different holes. Before buying, check that your wire or thread can pass through twice, because crimps and many weaves need a second pass. Carry a short piece of your usual wire to the shop and test a bead.
How beads are sold
**By strand:** many round beads come on a strand of about 40 cm (16 inches). Count is roughly 400 divided by the bead size in mm: about 100 beads of 4 mm, 66 of 6 mm or 50 of 8 mm.
**By pack or bag:** acrylic and crystal-style beads are often sold in bags of 100, 500 or by weight.
**By weight or tube:** seed beads are sold in grams, tubes or hanks (bundles of strung strands).
**Single pieces:** focal beads, pendants and natural coral are often priced one by one.

Buying beads well

Reading a beading wire label

Beading wire is sold on spools with two key numbers. The **strand count** (often 7, 19 or 49) tells you how many tiny steel wires are inside. More strands make the wire softer, more flexible and less likely to kink, so a necklace drapes nicely. 49-strand wire costs more; 7-strand is cheaper and stiffer, fine for practice and simple bracelets.

The **diameter** is often written in inches, for example .015 or .019. Thin wire (about .010 to .013) fits small-holed beads such as pearls. Medium wire (about .015 to .019) suits most glass and crystal pieces. Thick wire (about .024) suits heavy stones and large beads. A good rule: use the thickest wire that will still pass through your beads twice.
Avoid ordinary sewing thread and old fishing line

Sewing thread frays and snaps under the weight of glass beads. Some makers use nylon fishing line for bead bags, but monofilament line can stiffen and weaken with age and sunlight. If you use it, buy a fresh, good-quality line and test your finished work by pulling firmly.
Findings you will use every day
**Crimp beads and crimp tubes:** small soft metal beads squeezed onto beading wire to hold a clasp in place. Tubes give a neater, stronger hold than round crimp beads.
**Crimp covers:** round shells closed over a finished crimp so it looks like a small metal bead.
**Clasps:** lobster clasps (strong, common), toggle clasps (easy to open, good for bracelets), magnetic clasps (easy but can open with a hard pull).
**Jump rings:** small open metal rings that join a clasp to chain or to a loop. Split rings look like tiny key rings and are more secure.
**Head pins and eye pins:** short wires used to hang beads for earrings and charms.
**Wire guardians:** small curved tubes that protect beading wire where it rubs against the clasp.
**Extender chain:** a short chain at the back of a necklace so one size fits more customers.
**Bead stoppers:** small spring clips that stop beads sliding off while you work.

Metal quality and finishes

Findings come in base metal (often plated brass, iron or zinc alloy), stainless steel, sterling silver and gold-filled. Cheap plated findings can turn dark or green with sweat. Stainless steel resists rust and tarnish and is a good middle choice. Some people react to **nickel** in cheap metals with itchy, red skin. Only call your findings "nickel-free" or "hypoallergenic" if the supplier states it in writing.

Look after your eyes and back

Beading is close, detailed work. Sit at a table, not on the floor or bed, with your elbows supported and your work at a comfortable height. Use daylight from a window or a white LED lamp so colours look true. Eye doctors often recommend the 20-20-20 habit for close work: every 20 minutes, look at something about 20 feet (6 metres) away for 20 seconds. Stand up and stretch every hour.
Small parts and children

Beads, crimps and jump rings are choking hazards. Keep containers closed and out of reach of young children, sweep the floor after work, and never let a small child play with loose beads. Do not make bead necklaces for babies or toddlers: the US Food and Drug Administration has warned that teething necklaces can cause choking and strangulation.
Wire ends and glue

Cut wire pointing down into a bag or your palm, because short ends can fly off. Wear ordinary glasses or safety glasses when cutting. Use glue in a ventilated space with the cap on between uses, and keep it away from children.

A stretch bracelet is the best first project. It needs no clasp, uses few tools, and teaches the most important lesson in beadwork: **the finish decides the quality**. Most homemade stretch bracelets break because the cord was not pre-stretched, the knot was wrong, or the knot sat against a sharp bead edge. You will avoid all three.
A tied knot in cord
A properly tied and glued surgeon's knot is the heart of a stretch bracelet that lasts.
What you need
Clear or coloured elastic cord, 0.7 to 1 mm thick (thicker for heavier beads)
About 22 beads of 8 mm for an average adult bracelet, including one bead with a slightly larger hole to hide the knot
A bead stopper or a piece of tape
Small sharp scissors
Jewellery glue with a fine tip, such as G-S Hypo Cement
A tape measure
Step by step
Measure the wrist and add about 1.5 cm for an 8 mm bead bracelet. Write it down.
Cut about 30 cm of elastic so you have plenty of cord to hold when knotting.
Pre-stretch the cord: hold each end and pull firmly, a few times, along its whole length. This takes out the first stretch so the bracelet does not sag after a few days.
Clip a bead stopper or tape about 8 cm from one end.
Thread your beads in your planned pattern. Lay the strung beads around the tape measure to check the length.
Remove the stopper and tie the surgeon's knot (below). Pull each end firmly so the knot tightens and the beads sit close without gaps.
Put one small dot of glue on the knot and let it sit for a minute.
Slide the knot inside the large-hole bead next to it, if it fits, then trim the ends to about 3 mm. Leave the bracelet to dry flat for a few hours before wearing.
Tying the surgeon's knot

The surgeon's knot is like the first half of a reef knot with an extra wrap. Hold the left end in your left hand and the right end in your right. Cross the right end over the left and **wrap it through twice**. Pull both ends to tighten. Then cross left over right and wrap through **once**. Pull hard on both ends, and also pull the beads on each side apart a little to lock it. The double wrap grips the slippery elastic so the knot does not slide open.

Glue choice

Use a jewellery cement made for knots and use only a tiny amount. Many beaders avoid quick superglue on elastic because it can make the cord hard and brittle at the knot, which is where it then snaps.
Protect the cord from sharp holes

Faceted crystal and some metal beads have sharp hole edges that slowly cut elastic. Place a smooth bead or a small seed bead on either side of sharp beads, or double the cord by passing through twice.

A necklace with a proper clasp looks and sells as a finished product. The key skill is **crimping**: squeezing a small metal tube onto beading wire so the wire cannot slip out. Done well, a crimp holds for years. Done badly, by flattening it with ordinary pliers, it can slide open and drop every bead on the floor.

Crimping step by step
Thread one crimp tube onto the wire, then a wire guardian if you use one, then the loop of the clasp.
Bring the short end of the wire back down through the crimp tube, so both wires lie side by side inside it. Leave a tail of about 3 cm.
Slide the crimp tube up until there is a small, loose loop of wire around the clasp. Do not pull it so tight that the clasp cannot move.

Place the tube in the **back notch** of the crimping pliers (the one with a dip, nearest the handle). Make sure the two wires are not crossed. Squeeze firmly. The tube now has a groove with one wire on each side.
Turn the tube a quarter turn and place it in the **front notch** (the round one). Squeeze to fold the tube in half along the groove, making a neat, firm shape.
Tug the wire and clasp hard. If anything moves, cut off and redo it with a new crimp.
String your beads over both the wire and the tail for the first few beads, then trim the tail close.

At the other end, string a second crimp tube, a wire guardian if used, and the jump ring with the extender chain. Pass the wire back through the crimp tube and a few beads. Before crimping, **hold the necklace up in a curve**. If the beads stand stiffly like a bangle, loosen slightly. A necklace needs a little ease, about the width of half a bead, so it drapes softly. Then crimp and trim.

To hide the crimp, place a crimp cover over it in the front notch of the crimping pliers and close it gently until it looks like a small round metal bead. Squeeze a little at a time, turning it, so it does not crack.

Simple-loop earrings
Thread one or three beads onto a head pin.

Open rings sideways
Always open jump rings and loops by twisting one side towards you and the other away. Pulling them open into a C shape weakens the metal and leaves a gap that catches hair and lets parts fall off.

Bead bags and purses are popular for weddings, owambe parties and gifts, and they sell at higher prices than single strands. Many are made with **right-angle weave (RAW)**, a stitch where each unit is a small square of four beads and every bead sits at a right angle to its neighbours. The result is a flexible, net-like fabric that can be shaped into a bag, a box, a coaster or a napkin ring.
A handbag
A small beaded purse is built from hundreds of tiny four-bead squares joined together.
Materials for practice and for bags
For practice: 6 mm or 8 mm round or crystal-style beads in two colours, so you can see the pattern clearly
Strong line: many bag makers use clear nylon line or a braided beading thread; braided thread resists cutting by crystal edges
Two beading needles, or stiffen the two ends of the line with a dot of clear nail varnish

Two-needle cross-weave, step by step
Cut about 2 metres of line and put a needle on each end. Pick up 4 beads and slide them to the middle.
Pass the left needle through the 4th bead from the opposite direction, so the two ends cross inside it. Pull both ends firmly. You now have a square of four beads: your first unit.
On the right needle pick up 2 beads. On the left needle pick up 1 bead.
Pass the left needle through the second (outer) bead on the right needle, crossing again. Pull firmly. That is your second unit, sharing one bead with the first.
Repeat steps 3 and 4 until the strip is the width you want.
To start the next row, turn the work and use the side beads of the first row as the shared beads for each new unit, adding fewer beads each time because one or two sides already exist.

Keep the tension even: pull each cross firmly, but not so hard that the strip curls. If your units look like diamonds instead of squares, you are pulling unevenly between the two needles. Count every unit; writing your pattern in a grid on squared paper makes this much easier.
From strip to bag

A simple flat bag is two panels of RAW joined at the sides and bottom, or one long panel folded in half. Sides are joined by weaving through the edge beads of both panels with new connecting beads. A fabric lining stitched inside stops items falling through and makes the bag stronger. Finish with a strap: a beaded rope or a ready-made chain attached with jump rings.

Good technique is not enough on its own: pieces must look good together, pass a quality check every time, and be priced so you actually make money. This module covers colour and design, a finishing and honesty standard, and a step-by-step costing method in naira.

Two necklaces can use the same beads and the same technique, yet one looks expensive and the other looks random. The difference is **design**: which colours you put together, in what amounts, and in what pattern. You do not need art school. A colour wheel and a few simple rules will lift your work quickly.

The colour wheel in two minutes

The colour wheel arranges colours in a circle: the three **primary** colours (red, yellow, blue), the **secondary** colours made by mixing two primaries (orange, green, purple), and the in-between **tertiary** colours such as red-orange or blue-green. Three more words help: **hue** is the colour itself, **value** is how light or dark it is, and **saturation** is how bright or dull it is.

Neutrals such as gold, silver, black, white, cream and brown are your friends. They sit between strong colours, give the eye a rest and make bright beads stand out. A gold spacer between every few coloured beads is a classic Nigerian party look for good reason.
How much of each colour

A helpful starting rule used by many designers is roughly **60-30-10**: about 60% of the beads in a main colour, 30% in a second colour and 10% in an accent. Equal amounts of two strong colours often fight each other. Count it out on your bead mat before stringing.

Pattern, focal point and symmetry
**Repeat pattern:** a short sequence repeated along the strand, such as A-A-B-spacer. Write it down so you can make the same piece again.
**Focal point:** one larger or special bead or pendant at the centre front, where the eye lands first.
**Symmetry:** both sides of a necklace mirror each other from the centre. Lay out the centre first, then build out both sides at the same time.
**Graduation:** beads get gradually bigger towards the centre, which looks classic and flattering.
**Texture:** mixing shiny crystal with matte or metal beads adds interest even in one colour.
Check colour in daylight

Bead colours look different under a yellow bulb, a white LED and sunlight. Lay out your design near a window in daylight before stringing, and take a phone photo. If the photo looks muddy, the colours may be too close in value: add a lighter or darker bead.
Designing for the person and the occasion

Think about who will wear the piece and where. Office wear usually works best with smaller beads (4 to 6 mm), quieter colours and princess length, so it does not swing onto a keyboard. Party and wedding pieces can be bolder: larger focal beads, more sparkle and stronger contrast. Older customers often prefer lighter pieces that do not pull on the neck, so consider acrylic or smaller glass for long necklaces. Men's bracelets usually look best in matte, wood or dark stone-look beads with little sparkle.

Skin tone and clothing matter too. Bright, saturated colours such as gold, coral red, emerald and cobalt blue stand out beautifully on dark skin. When you design for an outfit, match one colour exactly and use the colour wheel to choose the others, rather than trying to match every colour in the fabric.

A customer judges your work in two moments: when she first sees it, and three weeks later when she has worn it to church, to work and to a party. A quality standard protects both moments. It also protects your name, because in a WhatsApp world one broken necklace can be shared with fifty people.
A person ticking items on a checklist
A written checklist makes every piece meet the same standard, not just the ones you made carefully.
The finishing checklist
**Connections:** every crimp is folded, firm and covered; every knot is glued and hidden; every jump ring is fully closed with no gap.
**Ends:** no sharp wire tails that scratch skin; trimmed thread ends are short and tucked.
**Beads:** no chipped, cracked, scratched or peeling beads; pattern matches the plan with no mistakes.
**Fit and drape:** correct length for the order; necklace curves softly; bracelet rolls on without strain.
**Look:** symmetrical from the centre; clasp sits at the back; nothing twisted.
**Clean:** no glue marks, fingerprints or fluff; polished with a soft dry cloth.

Every fault you record and fix makes the next batch stronger.
Three simple tests
**Tug test:** hold the clasp in one hand and the beads near it in the other and pull firmly. Repeat at the other end. Nothing should move or slip.
**Drape test:** hold the necklace up by the clasp and let it hang, then lay it on a curved surface such as a rolled towel. It should curve smoothly with no stiff sections or gaps.
**Wear test:** for each new design or material, wear one piece yourself (or ask a friend to) for at least a week of normal life. Note any loosening, colour rub-off, tarnish or skin irritation.

For example, Ifeoma in Onitsha makes 20 bracelets with new metallic-coated beads for a market day.

She records the fault: 'Coated beads, supplier X, coating rubs off with sweat in under a week.'
She sells the remaining bracelets only as 'fashion pieces for occasional wear' at a lower price, and stops buying that bead.
She asks her supplier for a sturdier finish and tests the new sample before buying in bulk.
Instead of twenty unhappy customers, she has one honest product description and a better supplier.

Call materials what they are. Say "glass crystal beads", not "Swarovski", unless you bought genuine branded crystals with proof. Say "coral-style beads" or "imitation coral" unless you know the coral is real. Say "gold-tone" or "gold-plated", not "gold". Only say "nickel-free", "hypoallergenic" or "stainless steel" when the supplier confirms it in writing. Honest wording builds repeat customers and avoids disputes.

Children's and babies' jewellery

Small beads and parts are choking hazards. Do not make teething necklaces or bead jewellery for babies; the US FDA has warned of choking and strangulation risks. For older children, use large beads, stretch cord that breaks away rather than strong wire around the neck, and tell parents the piece is not for children under three.

Write your checklist on a card and keep it on your work table. Tick it for every piece, not only for orders that feel important. A consistent standard means your cheapest bracelet and your most expensive bead bag both carry your name with pride.

Storage is part of quality too. Keep finished pieces flat or hanging, in separate pouches or bags, so crystals do not scratch each other and chains do not tangle. Keep them away from damp, direct sunlight and perfume, which can dull coatings and tarnish plated metal.
Respecting other designers

Learning from tutorials and copying a technique such as right-angle weave is normal. Copying a specific designer's distinctive piece exactly and selling it as your own is not fair practice, and can harm your reputation. Use what you learn, then change colours, proportions and details until the design is yours.

Many beaders lose money without knowing it. They count the beads, forget the clasp, the wire, the pouch, the transport to the market and their own time, then charge what a friend says is fair. A simple costing method fixes this. All naira figures in this lesson are **approximate examples**; prices change often, so always use your own current receipts.
An abacus for counting
Careful counting of every cost is what turns a hobby into a business.
Step 1: cost per unit of each material

You buy in bulk but use small amounts, so first work out the cost of **one** unit. Divide the price you paid by how many you got. A pack of 100 beads for 2,000 naira is 20 naira per bead. A 10-metre roll of wire for 3,000 naira is 300 naira per metre, or 3 naira per centimetre. Keep these unit costs in a notebook or a simple spreadsheet and update them when you restock.
Step 2: build the full cost
**Materials:** every bead, spacer, wire or cord, crimp, cover, clasp, jump ring and extender.
**Labour:** your time. Choose an hourly rate you think is fair locally and use it every time. Time yourself making the piece.
**Packaging:** pouch, box, card, sticker or label.

**Overheads:** costs that are not in one piece but are real: transport to buy materials, data for WhatsApp selling, tool replacement, broken beads. A simple method is to add a percentage, such as 10% of material cost.
Worked example: costing a crystal necklace (approximate prices)
For example, Kemi in Lagos makes a 45 cm necklace of 6 mm glass crystals with gold-tone spacers. All prices are approximate examples, not market quotes.
Crystals: 66 beads from a pack of 100 for about 2,000 naira = 66 x 20 = about 1,320 naira.
Spacers: 16 from a pack of 100 for about 1,000 naira = 16 x 10 = about 160 naira.
Wire: 60 cm at about 3 naira per cm = about 180 naira.
Findings: 2 crimp tubes, 2 covers, clasp, jump ring and extender chain = about 400 naira.
Material total: 1,320 + 160 + 180 + 400 = about 2,060 naira.
Labour: 1 hour at her chosen rate of 1,000 naira per hour = 1,000 naira.
Packaging: organza pouch and card = about 250 naira.
Overheads: 10% of materials = about 206 naira.
Full cost: 2,060 + 1,000 + 250 + 206 = about 3,516 naira.
Her full cost is about 3,500 naira. Any price below that loses money, even if it feels like a sale.
Step 3: add profit and set prices

Profit is separate from your labour. Labour pays you for your time; profit lets the business grow, buy more stock and survive slow months. Many small makers add a profit margin of 30% to 50% on top of full cost for retail. For Kemi, full cost of about 3,516 plus 40% profit (about 1,406) gives about 4,922 naira, which she rounds to **5,000 naira retail**.

A **wholesale price** is for people who buy several pieces to resell, such as a boutique or a reseller on Instagram. It must still be above your full cost, but leaves room for their profit. Kemi might set wholesale at full cost plus 15% to 20%, about 4,000 to 4,200 naira, with a minimum order of five pieces. Never sell wholesale below full cost.

Step 4: check the market

Now compare. Look at similar pieces at your local market, on Instagram and in WhatsApp status updates from other sellers. If your price is far above theirs, ask why: are your materials better, is your finish stronger, or are you slower? You can buy materials in larger quantities, speed up with practice, simplify the design or target customers who value quality. If your price is far below, you may be underpricing your skill.

Review your prices every time you restock. If a pack of beads that cost 2,000 naira now costs 2,500, your unit cost per bead rises from 20 to 25 naira, and every piece using that bead costs more to make. Update your costing sheet first, then decide whether to raise the price, change the design or find a better supplier. Tell regular customers politely about price changes in advance.

Growing your income further

Choose one direction for your next 90 days rather than all at once. Test it, track your weekly numbers, and decide at the end of the period whether to continue, adjust or try another direction. This simple rhythm of plan, act, measure and decide is what turns a craft into a dependable income.

Most beads are measured in millimetres across the widest part.

Choose the finished length
Subtract the clasp length

Step two. Take away the length of the clasp, jump ring and crimps, because beads do not fill that part.
Step three. Divide what is left by the size of one bead.

Choosing a string
Beading wire is tiny steel wires twisted together and coated in nylon. It lasts longer and holds heavy beads. You finish it with crimps and crimping pliers.
More strands inside, such as 49, means a softer drape. Use the thickest wire that still passes through your beads twice.
Elastic cord is fast and cheap and needs no clasp, but it can stretch out over time. Use it for light beads, finished with a surgeon's knot and a dot of glue.
Do not use sewing thread. It frays and snaps under the weight of glass beads.

In beadwork, the finish decides the quality. Most homemade stretch bracelets break because the cord was not pre-stretched, the knot was wrong, or the knot sat against a sharp bead edge.

Project one
Your first stretch bracelet
Measure the wrist, add about 1.5 cm
Cut about 30 cm of elastic
Pre-stretch the whole cord
Thread beads, check the length
Surgeon's knot, tiny glue dot, hide it
Pre-stretch first. Use jewellery cement, not quick superglue.
Step one. Measure the wrist and add about 1.5 cm for 8 mm beads.
Step two. Cut about 30 cm of elastic.
Step three. Hold each end and pull firmly, a few times, along the whole length. This takes out the first stretch, so the bracelet does not sag after a few days.
Step four. Thread your beads and check the length against the tape measure.
Step five. Tie the surgeon's knot. Cross right over left and wrap through twice. Then left over right, once. Pull hard.

Project two
Crimping a clasp in two steps
Crimp tube, then the clasp loop
Wire back down through the tube
Back notch: make the groove
Front notch: fold it in half
Tug hard. If it moves, redo it
Never flatten a crimp with ordinary pliers.
Thread one crimp tube onto the wire, then the loop of the clasp.
Bring the short end back down through the tube, so both wires lie side by side. Leave a tail of about 3 cm and a small, loose loop around the clasp.
Place the tube in the back notch of the crimping pliers, the one with a dip, nearest the handle. Check the wires are not crossed, and squeeze. Now there is a groove.
Turn the tube a quarter turn, place it in the front notch, the round one, and squeeze to fold it in half.
Tug the wire and clasp hard. If anything moves, cut it off and redo it with a new crimp. Flattening a crimp with ordinary pliers is the mistake that drops beads on the floor.

Right way, wrong way
Do

Twist jump rings open sideways

Right-angle weave in brief
Each unit is a square of 4 beads
Two needles cross inside one bead

Many small makers add 30 to 50% for retail. Kemi adds about 40%, about 1,406 naira, and rounds to 5,000 naira retail.
Wholesale is for resellers. Kemi might set about 4,000 to 4,200 naira, with a minimum order of five pieces.
Compare with similar pieces at your market and online, and update your costing sheet every time you restock.
Selling below full cost means you pay to work. If a customer's budget is small, offer a simpler design with fewer or cheaper beads.

Plan and batch your collection
Pick a theme: colour, occasion or technique
Choose three to five pieces that go together
Count all beads first into separate lids
Do each stage across the whole batch
No new design until the old ones pass your checklist every time.
Step one. Choose a theme that links the pieces, such as a colour story like Emerald and Gold, an occasion, or a technique.
Step two. Choose three to five pieces that work together, like a necklace, bracelet and earrings. Sets raise the average sale.
Step three. Write a pattern card for each design: the bead list with exact counts, the pattern as letters, the findings, the time taken and the full cost.
Step four. Count out all the beads for all the pieces first, into separate small bowls or lids, one per piece. You notice at once if you are short.
Step five. Do each stage across the batch. String all, then knot or crimp all, then inspect all.
A small range made well sells better than a large range with uneven quality.
Worked example
Ngozi batches five bracelets
Count beads for all five: 15 min
String all five: 25 min
Knot and glue all five: 15 min
Batch 55 min instead of 75
Ngozi in Enugu takes about 15 minutes to make one bracelet from start to finish. Five, one by one, would take about 75 minutes.
In a batch, she spends 15 minutes counting beads for all five.
25 minutes stringing all five.
And 15 minutes knotting and gluing all five.
That is 55 minutes. She saves about 20 minutes per five bracelets, and all five come out identical. Her labour cost per piece drops, so her profit rises at the same price.
Phone photos
Photos that sell
Wipe the lens; daylight, no flash
Plain background, the same every time
Three photos: flat, close-up, worn
Do not change the colours
Wipe the camera lens. Work near a window in daylight, and avoid the flash, which causes glare on crystals.
Use a plain background, like white paper or a wooden board, and keep it the same for the whole collection.
Take three photos per piece: the whole piece laid flat, a close-up of the beads and clasp, and the piece worn to show size.
Crop and brighten a little, but never change the colours. The customer must receive what she saw.

Safe payments
Protect your money
Never release goods because of an SMS or a transfer screenshot.
Open your own banking or wallet app and confirm the money is in your balance.
Never share your PIN, password or one-time code, even with someone claiming to be your bank.
Fake bank alert messages and fake transfer screenshots are common. Never release goods because of an SMS or a screenshot.
Open your own banking or wallet app and confirm the money is really in your balance.
And never share your PIN, password or one-time code with anyone, including people who say they are from your bank.
